sections.title: Supporting planes and strong monotonicity
sections.intro:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space. We use the convention that \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is \(m\)-strongly convex when \(v\mapsto f(v)-m\|v\|^2/2\) is convex. For a differentiable convex function, restriction to a line segment gives the supporting-plane inequality. Applying it to the quadratic-subtracted function gives the quadratic lower bound. Applying the lower bound to \((x,y)\) and \((y,x)\), and adding, gives strong monotonicity of the gradient.

The derivative \(Df(x)\) is a continuous linear functional. In a Hilbert space it is represented by \(\nabla f(x)\), so \(Df(x)[v]=\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle\). These arguments require no second derivative or minimizer.

declarations.name: convex_first_order
declarations.title: The supporting-plane inequality
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and convex on all of \(H\). For any \(x,y\in H\),

\[f(x)+Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y).\]

steps.prose: Restrict \(f\) to the affine line \(\ell(t)=x+t(y-x)\). Since affine composition preserves convexity, \(\varphi=f\circ\ell\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\), with \(\varphi(0)=f(x)\) and \(\varphi(1)=f(y)\).
steps.note:
1. Line 20.

    Define an object. let line : ℝ →ᵃ[ℝ] H := AffineMap.lineMap x y introduces a local name line, available below this line until this proof ends. let gives a value a name; it does not assume a new theorem. The colon : means “has type.” ℝ is the type of real numbers; H is our vector space. The entire notation ℝ →ᵃ[ℝ] H means an affine map from the real line to H, over real scalars. The raised ᵃ is part of the notation, not an exponent or a variable named a. The bracketed ℝ records the scalar field, and the first ℝ records the domain. A plain ℝ → H would only say “function”; the affine-map type also bundles a proof that the function preserves affine combinations. An equivalent type is AffineMap ℝ ℝ H; see the typing guide for entering the notation.

    := means “is defined to be,” placing the value on the right. It is not the proposition =, and it is not an instruction to change an existing variable. AffineMap.lineMap is a case-sensitive library name: AffineMap is the namespace and lineMap the construction inside it. AffineMap.lineMap x y supplies its endpoint arguments in order: the value at zero is x, the value at one is y. Spaces apply a function to arguments; no comma or multiplication is implicit. Its value at t is t • (y - x) + x. Here • multiplies a vector by a scalar. We construct the whole affine line, not a map defined only on the segment. Lean automatically uses the underlying function when we write line t or compose with it.

  2. Line 21.

    State a small fact to prove now. have hc : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ (f ∘ line) := by creates a named local theorem hc. The pattern is have name : proposition := proof. Unlike the preceding let, the value being supplied here is a proof of the proposition after the colon. have does not grant the proposition for free: Lean opens a new goal and checks the indented proof that follows. Once that goal is solved, the main proof resumes with hc available. We choose the letters hc to suggest “hypothesis, convexity”; any unused ordinary identifier could have been used.

    ConvexOn takes the scalar field, set, and function in that order. Set.univ now means every real number, inferred from the domain of the composition. f ∘ line is the function sending t to f (line t). Parentheses group it as one argument. := by supplies a proof using tactics, and the extra indentation on the next line marks the body of this nested proof. At this moment the local goal is convexity of the restricted scalar function, while the original supporting-plane inequality is waiting outside the nested block.

  3. Line 22.

    Supply that proof after simplification. hf.comp_affineMap line invokes the library theorem ConvexOn.comp_affineMap with the existing convexity proof hf and the affine map line. This dot notation is convenient theorem application, not a change to hf. The theorem says that composing a convex function with an affine map preserves convexity on the preimage of the original set. Its set is initially the preimage of Set.univ, which simplifies to Set.univ.

    simpa [line] using ... means “simplify the type of the supplied proof and the current target, then use the proof when those types match.” using identifies the proof to start with. simpa combines simplification with closing the goal; simp alone only asks for simplification. The list [line] tells the simplifier to unfold the local definition line, replacing it by AffineMap.lineMap x y wherever needed. It is not an array, a singleton set, an assumption, or a request for a typeclass instance. The same bracket syntax after simp/simpa can contain definitions to unfold and equalities to rewrite with. Because there is no only, the usual simplifier rules also participate. Finishing this line finishes the proof of hc; the next line returns to the original indentation and original theorem goal.

steps.prose:
The derivative of the line is its constant direction:

\[\ell'(0)=y-x.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 23.

    have hl : HasDerivAt line (y - x) 0 := by names the next auxiliary theorem hl. Read HasDerivAt function derivative point in exactly that order: the function line has vector-valued derivative y - x at the real input zero. The three expressions are arguments separated by spaces. Parentheses keep y - x together. The point zero has type ℝ, inferred from the domain of line. The new nested goal is this derivative statement; proving it will add hl to the main context.

  2. Line 24.

    change replaces a goal with a definitionally equal spelling: Lean checks that unfolding definitions makes the old and new goals the same. It is not an assertion that arbitrary equal expressions may be exchanged without evidence. Here it exposes the underlying function of AffineMap.lineMap x y. In fun t : ℝ ↦ ..., fun introduces an anonymous function, t is its input name, the type annotation makes t real, and ↦ separates the input from the body. Thus the goal is visibly differentiation of t • (y - x) + x.

  3. Line 25.

    simpa using starts a tactic whose supplied proof continues on the next line. A newline does not end an expression that still needs an argument. This use has no explicit simplifier list, so it uses the library's default simplification rules. The elementary differentiation rules below produce a derivative expression containing the scalar one; simplification identifies it with y - x. We do not have to type the derivative proof as one very long line.

  4. Line 26.

    hasDerivAt_id (0 : ℝ) proves that the identity function has derivative one at zero. (0 : ℝ) is a type ascription: it disambiguates which kind of zero is intended. .smul_const (y - x) differentiates the identity function multiplied by the fixed vector y - x; .add_const x then differentiates the result plus the fixed vector x. Parentheses select the intermediate proof to which each dot operation applies. These theorems assemble an actual proof term, which the preceding simpa converts to our target. Constants have derivative zero, leaving the direction vector.

steps.prose:
By the chain rule, the derivative of the restricted function is

\[\varphi'(0)=Df(x)[y-x].\]
steps.note:
1. Line 27.

    have hd : HasDerivAt (f ∘ line) (fderiv ℝ f x (y - x)) 0 := by asks for the chain-rule derivative of the composition. As before, HasDerivAt lists function, proposed derivative, and input point. The function is now real-valued, so the proposed derivative is a real number. fderiv ℝ f x is the continuous linear derivative of f at the vector x; its final application to (y - x) evaluates the directional derivative. This is not multiplication of four quantities. The declared name hd will be used in the convex slope theorem.

  2. Line 28.

    exact closes the goal by providing a proof whose type matches it. hdiff x specializes the global differentiability hypothesis at x; .hasFDerivAt turns that into a derivative statement with the canonical derivative fderiv ℝ f x. The theorem .comp_hasDerivAt_of_eq is a chain rule allowing the outer derivative point to be identified by an equality. Its arguments here are the inner input 0, the line-derivative proof hl, and a proof that line 0 = x. The parenthesized (by simp [line]) is a complete little tactic proof supplied as that last argument: unfold line, evaluate the endpoint, and close the equality. It does not start a new standalone theorem. The chain rule applies the linear derivative of f to the direction y - x, producing exactly the scalar named in hd.

steps.prose:
For a differentiable convex function, the derivative at the left endpoint is bounded by the secant slope to a later point. Applying this at \(0<1\) gives

\[Df(x)[y-x]\le\frac{\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)}{1-0}.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 29.

    have hs := ... omits a colon and an explicitly written proposition. Lean infers the type of hs from the proof on the right of :=; it is still a rigorously checked local theorem. hc.le_slope_of_hasDerivAt uses the convexity proof hc to compare a derivative with a secant slope. The dot supplies hc to the theorem; subsequent spaces supply further arguments. Set.mem_univ 0 and Set.mem_univ 1 are proofs that the real endpoints zero and one lie in the universal set. They are membership proofs, rather than numerical values to substitute into the inequality. The function and derivative value are inferred from hc and the derivative proof supplied next.

  2. Line 30.

    This indented continuation supplies the two remaining arguments of the same application. zero_lt_one proves strict positivity of one; : (0 : ℝ) < 1 explicitly asks Lean to use its real-number instance. The inner annotation fixes the type of zero, while the outer annotation fixes the proposition proved. hd supplies the derivative at zero from the preceding block. The library theorem needs an ordered pair of distinct endpoints, hence the strict inequality rather than just 0 ≤ 1. The new fact hs says that the directional derivative is bounded by the slope of f ∘ line between zero and one. The original supporting-plane goal remains unchanged until we simplify this intermediate fact.

steps.prose:
Evaluate the two endpoints and rearrange:

\[Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y)-f(x),\qquad f(x)+Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y).\]
steps.note:
1. Line 31.

    simp only [ ... ] at hs simplifies the proposition stored under hs, leaving the main goal alone. only restricts the named simplification rules, rather than also using the normal global simp set; Lean still performs basic definitional reductions. slope_def_field writes the secant slope as a difference quotient; Function.comp_apply turns application of a composition into nested application. line unfolds the local definition. AffineMap.lineMap_apply_one evaluates the line at one as y. The opening bracket begins a list that continues on the next physical line; no tactic finishes here.

  2. Line 32.

    AffineMap.lineMap_apply_zero evaluates the other endpoint as x; sub_zero simplifies 1 - 0; div_one removes division by one. The closing ] ends the list, and at hs identifies the local hypothesis to replace by its simplified form. After this instruction, hs expresses fderiv ℝ f x (y - x) ≤ f y - f x. Names such as sub_zero are library equalities; line is a local definition. Both can appear in the same simplifier list, with different roles.

  3. Line 33.

    linarith is a tactic for linear arithmetic consequences of equalities and inequalities in the current context. It uses the simplified hs to move f x to the left and prove f x + fderiv ℝ f x (y - x) ≤ f y. It treats the complicated derivative expression as a single real quantity; it does not prove the calculus or convexity steps itself. There is no remaining nested goal: this closes the original theorem. The tactic generates a proof checked by Lean, so invoking automation does not add an assumption.

declarations.statement_note:
lemma introduces a proved declaration; its name is the label used to invoke it later. {f : H → ℝ} is an implicit function argument: f takes a vector and returns a real number. (hf : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ f) names a proof of convexity, over real scalars, on Set.univ, the whole space. (hdiff : Differentiable ℝ f) names a proof that f is differentiable everywhere; hdiff x specializes it at x. Names beginning with h are a convention for hypotheses, not a special Lean syntax.

(x y : H) introduces two explicit vector arguments. The colon after the binders starts the conclusion. f x means function application, and fderiv ℝ f x (y - x) means: take the real Fréchet derivative of f at x, then apply that linear map to y - x. The inequality is the goal. := by begins its tactic proof. The first lemma needs no CompleteSpace H assumption because it uses a derivative, rather than its representation by a gradient.

declarations.name: strong_gradient_monotone
declarations.title: Strong monotonicity of the gradient
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. If \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, where \(m\in\mathbb R\), then for every \(x,y\in H\),

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle.\]

steps.prose:
Set

\[g(v)=f(v)-\frac m2\|v\|^2.\]

By the definition of strong convexity, \(g\) is convex.
steps.note:
1. Line 39.

    let g : H → ℝ := fun v ↦ ... names the shifted function locally. H → ℝ specifies its input and output types. fun v ↦ binds a fresh input v in the formula; it is not a claim for just one particular vector. f v - m / 2 * ‖v‖ ^ 2 subtracts the strong-convexity quadratic. Ordinary arithmetic precedence makes the power bind first, and the division/multiplication form the coefficient multiplying that square. The definition is immutable and can later be unfolded with simp [g] or dsimp [g].

  2. Line 40.

    have hc : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ g := ... gives a proof name to convexity of g. The theorem strongConvexOn_iff_convex is an equivalence between strong convexity of f and convexity of this particular quadratic shift. .mp takes the forward implication of an “if and only if” theorem; applying it to hsc produces the required convexity proof. := is followed directly by a proof expression here, so no nested by block is necessary. Lean unfolds the local definition g as needed when checking the type. The remaining main goal is still strong monotonicity of the original gradient.

steps.prose:
The squared norm has derivative \(D\|v\|^2[u]=2\langle v,u\rangle\). Consequently \(g\) is differentiable and

\[Dg(v)[u]=Df(v)[u]-m\langle v,u\rangle.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 41.

    have hg (v : H) : HasFDerivAt g begins a local theorem with a parameter. Once proved, hg can be applied to any vector, for example hg x and hg y. HasFDerivAt states that a specified continuous linear map is the Fréchet derivative, rather than a one-variable scalar derivative. The proposition is incomplete until the next line supplies the map and point. (v : H) is an explicit local binder, and its scope includes this theorem's type and nested proof.

  2. Line 42.

    The proposed derivative is fderiv ℝ f v - (m / 2) • (2 • innerSL ℝ v), evaluated at the base point v. innerSL ℝ v bundles the continuous linear functional sending a direction u to inner ℝ v u. The inner scalar multiplication gives the derivative of the squared norm, and the outer one multiplies it by m / 2. Subtraction here is subtraction of linear maps, not vector subtraction in H. The last v is the point of differentiation. := by opens the proof of this formula.

  3. Line 43.

    (hdiff v).hasFDerivAt provides the derivative of f at this v. Its .sub operation is the differentiation rule for the difference of two functions. exact will finish the local theorem once the second function's derivative proof is supplied by the following continuation. The proof of differentiability hdiff is a function-like universal statement, which is why it can be specialized by writing hdiff v.

  4. Line 44.

    hasStrictFDerivAt_norm_sq v is the library derivative formula for the squared norm. Strict differentiability is stronger than the ordinary differentiability needed here, so .hasFDerivAt forgets the stronger part. .const_mul (m / 2) applies the rule for a real constant times a real-valued function. The resulting proof is the second argument to .sub above. Lean checks the resulting derivative map against the formula in hg; the local definition of g makes the underlying function match.

  5. Line 45.

    have hgd : Differentiable ℝ g := fun v ↦ (hg v).differentiableAt packages pointwise derivative existence into global differentiability. fun v ↦ constructs a proof for every point v; hg v supplies our explicit derivative formula there, and .differentiableAt retains only existence of a derivative. hgd will satisfy the differentiability argument of convex_first_order. This line supplies a proof term directly after :=, illustrating that anonymous functions can construct proofs as well as numerical functions.

steps.prose:
Apply the supporting-plane inequality in both directions, and substitute the derivative just computed:

\[g(x)+Dg(x)[y-x]\le g(y),\qquad g(y)+Dg(y)[x-y]\le g(x).\]
steps.note:
1. Line 46.

    have hxy := convex_first_order hc hgd x y applies the previous lemma to the shifted function. Lean infers its implicit f as g from hc and hgd. The explicit arguments provide convexity, differentiability, base point x, and comparison point y, in that order. The inferred type of hxy is the supporting-plane inequality involving g x, g y, and fderiv ℝ g x (y - x).

  2. Line 47.

    have hyx := convex_first_order hc hgd y x invokes the same lemma with the points reversed. This is a second proof, rather than a rename of hxy. Its derivative is based at y and acts on x - y. Keeping both facts in the context lets a later arithmetic tactic add their inequalities and cancel the function values.

  3. Line 48.

    rw [(hg x).fderiv] at hxy rewrites the derivative inside the local fact hxy. hg x proves the derivative formula at x; .fderiv extracts the equality identifying the canonical map fderiv ℝ g x with that explicit derivative. rw means rewrite, the brackets hold the equality to use, and at hxy directs the change to that hypothesis. It does not change the main goal.

  4. Line 49.

    rw [(hg y).fderiv] at hyx performs the matching substitution for the other supporting plane. The base point matters: a formula at x would not justify replacing the derivative at y. After these two lines, both local inequalities contain known linear maps derived from f and the quadratic correction, ready to evaluate on their respective displacement vectors.

steps.prose:
Express the derivative of \(f\) using its gradient. The two inequalities become

\[\begin{aligned}f(x)-\tfrac m2\|x\|^2+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle-m\langle x,y-x\rangle&\le f(y)-\tfrac m2\|y\|^2,\\ f(y)-\tfrac m2\|y\|^2+\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle-m\langle y,x-y\rangle&\le f(x)-\tfrac m2\|x\|^2.\end{aligned}\]
steps.note:
1. Line 50.

    simp only [g, sub_apply, smul_apply, ...] begins simplification of the two supporting-plane facts. g unfolds the shifted function. sub_apply evaluates the subtraction of two functions/maps at an argument, so the derivative-map difference becomes a difference of scalar values. smul_apply similarly evaluates a scalar multiple of a map at an argument. The comma-separated bracket list continues onto the next line; this is one tactic, not two independent simplifications.

  2. Line 51.

    smul_eq_mul replaces scalar action on real numbers by ordinary multiplication. innerSL_apply_apply evaluates the bundled inner-product functional. ← inner_gradient_left uses the inner-product/derivative identity backwards, turning the linear derivative applied to a direction into an inner product with the gradient. The left arrow reverses the usual orientation of that rewrite rule; it is not a logical implication. at hxy hyx applies the whole simplification to both named hypotheses, preserving the main goal. We now have concrete real inequalities in function values, norms, and inner products, with the abstract derivative maps eliminated. The normal simplifier set is excluded by only, keeping the intended conversion explicit.

steps.prose:
Add these inequalities. The function values and quadratic values cancel. Using \(\langle x-y,x-y\rangle=\|x-y\|^2\), what remains is

\[0\le\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle-m\|x-y\|^2.\]

This is the required monotonicity inequality.
steps.note:
1. Line 52.

    rw [inner_sub_left, inner_sub_right, inner_sub_right] rewrites the main goal because no at target is present. The first rule distributes the inner product over its left difference of gradients; the next two distribute over the right displacement in the resulting two terms. Repeating a rule matters: rw follows the ordered list rather than globally applying all possible rewrites until nothing remains.

  2. Line 53.

    rw [norm_sub_sq_real] expands the squared distance in the main goal into squared norms and a cross inner product. This is a Hilbert-space identity; the arithmetic tactic below cannot derive vector geometry itself. The equality supplies the bridge from the norm expression to scalar polynomial arithmetic.

  3. Line 54.

    simp only [inner_sub_right, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, two_smul, ...] continues the normalization. The rules distribute inner products over a difference, replace a vector's self-inner-product by its squared norm, and interpret multiplication by two as addition where relevant. The bracketed list is unfinished until the next line.

  4. Line 55.

    real_inner_comm makes real inner products symmetric in a consistent direction. at hxy hyx ⊢ applies the listed simplifications to the two hypotheses and to the current goal; ⊢ is the goal marker used as a tactic target, not an additional theorem. This ensures that the same real quantities occur in all three expressions, so the arithmetic tool can recognize their cancellations.

  5. Line 56.

    nlinarith finishes by polynomial arithmetic on the normalized real expressions. It uses hxy and hyx, whose function values cancel, leaving precisely the desired comparison with m * ‖x - y‖ ^ 2. Compared with linarith, it can also handle polynomial products and powers arising from the norm expansion. It does not invent the supporting-plane or derivative identities: those have already been supplied as checked facts.

declarations.statement_note:
[CompleteSpace H] adds the completeness assumption needed to represent real continuous linear functionals by gradient vectors. It is an instance binder: Lean searches for a suitable instance when the lemma is applied. {f : H → ℝ} and {m : ℝ} are inferred arguments. The explicit proof inputs are hdiff, differentiability everywhere, and hsc : StrongConvexOn Set.univ m f, strong convexity on all of H with Mathlib's m / 2 normalization. The statement permits any real m; positivity is not silently assumed.

gradient f x is a vector in H. inner ℝ (gradient f x - gradient f y) (x - y) is the real inner product of the gradient difference and point difference. * is real multiplication, ^ 2 is squaring, and ‖x - y‖ is a real norm. The goal is the displayed real inequality, proved using two supporting planes for a shifted function.

steps.prose:
Collect the quadratic correction by the identity

\[\|y\|^2-\|x\|^2-2\langle x,y-x\rangle=\|y-x\|^2.\]

Moving terms gives the desired lower model.
steps.note:
1. Line 75.

    rw [norm_sub_sq_real] expands the squared displacement occurring in the target lower-model inequality. Because there is no at clause, it changes the main goal rather than the supporting-plane fact. The rule expresses a squared distance using squared norms and a real cross inner product. Lean needs this geometric identity explicitly before real arithmetic can collect the terms.

    simp only [inner_sub_right, real_inner_comm] at hxy ⊢ normalizes the same inner-product expressions in the local fact and goal. inner_sub_right distributes over subtraction in the second slot; real_inner_comm swaps arguments of real inner products to make matching terms recognizable. hxy is the known inequality and ⊢ marks the goal. sections.title: The quadratic upper model
sections.intro: Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(L\ge0\). For \(d=y-x\), the derivative along \(x+td\) is \(\langle\nabla f(x+td),d\rangle\). Its difference from \(\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\) is at most \(Lt\|d\|^2\) on \([0,1]\). Integrating gives the quadratic upper bound with remainder \(L\|d\|^2/2\). The proof below also obtains this bound by showing that the segment function minus this quadratic is nonincreasing. Neither argument assumes a Hessian.

declarations.name: smooth_upper_bound
declarations.title: The descent lemma
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(L\ge0\). Suppose \(f:H o\mathbb R\) is differentiable and

\[\| abla f(u)- abla f(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|\quad(u,v\in H).\]

Then for every \(x,y\),

\[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+ rac L2\|y-x\|^2.\]

steps.prose:
Set \(d=y-x\), \(a=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\), \(b=\|d\|^2\), and define the segment function

\[q(t)=f(x+td)-f(x)-ta-\frac L2t^2b.\]

It suffices to show \(q(1)\le q(0)=0\).

For \(t\) in the interior of \([0,1]\), we have \(t\ge0\). Lipschitz continuity gives

sections.title: A first Euler-step estimate
sections.intro:
Let \(d=x-y\) and \(v=g_x-g_y\), where the supplied vectors satisfy \(m\|d\|^2\le\langle v,d angle\) and \(\|v\|\le L\|d\|\). For \(h\ge0\), expanding \(\|d-hv\|^2\) and applying these two inequalities gives the coefficient \(1-2hm+h^2L^2\). Taking nonnegative square roots gives the norm estimate. The vectors need not be gradients; their substitution by \( abla U(x)\) and \( abla U(y)\) is a specialization.

If \(d=0\), the Lipschitz hypothesis forces \(v=0\). If \(d e0\), the squared estimate implies that its scalar coefficient is nonnegative. Thus the square-root conclusion needs no separate sign hypothesis on that coefficient.

declarations.name: gradient_step_sq_bound
declarations.title: The squared Euler-step bound
declarations.statement:
Let \(x,y,g_x,g_y\) lie in a real inner-product space, let \(m\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and \(h\ge0\). Assume

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle,\qquad\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|.\]

Then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|^2\le(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\|x-y\|^2.\]

steps.prose:
Both sides of the Lipschitz estimate are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality:

\[\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le L^2\|x-y\|^2.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 23.

    have hLipSq : ... := by states the squared version of the input Lipschitz bound. The square of the product on its original right side has been written as (L : ℝ) ^ 2 * ‖x - y‖ ^ 2. Squaring an inequality is not valid without appropriate sign information, so this is a theorem to prove, not a syntactic rewrite of hLip. The local proof uses the nonnegative norms and the stored sign of L.

  2. Line 24.

    nlinarith [norm_nonneg (gx - gy), norm_nonneg (x - y), L.coe_nonneg] supplies three extra facts to polynomial arithmetic. The first two state that the respective norms are nonnegative; L.coe_nonneg gives 0 ≤ (L : ℝ) from the nonnegative-real object. The tactic also sees the original hypothesis hLip, and uses these signs to justify the squared comparison. These brackets are extra arithmetic premises, whereas brackets after simp specify simplification instructions. After this nested proof closes, hLipSq is available as a checked fact in the main proof.

steps.prose:
Multiply strong monotonicity by \(2h\ge0\), and multiply the squared Lipschitz estimate by \(h^2\ge0\):

\[2hm\|x-y\|^2\le2h\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle,\qquad h^2\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le h^2L^2\|x-y\|^2.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 25.

    mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hmono ... multiplies both sides of hmono by the same nonnegative factor on the left. show 0 ≤ 2 * h by positivity is an inline proof of the required sign. show specifies its proposition; positivity combines hh with the positive numeral two. The resulting local theorem hmonoScaled contains the factor 2 * h that will occur in the squared-norm expansion. have ... := lets Lean infer that entire inequality's type.

  2. Line 26.

    mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hLipSq (sq_nonneg h) similarly multiplies the squared Lipschitz inequality by h ^ 2. sq_nonneg h is the general real-number fact that a square is nonnegative, so this scaling needs no additional hypothesis. The result is named hLipScaled. Both prepared inequalities are aligned with coefficients that appear after expansion; the eventual arithmetic tactic cannot safely multiply ordered inequalities by unknown-sign factors without these explicit sign proofs.

steps.prose:
Write \(d=x-y\), \(v=g_x-g_y\). Expanding the squared norm and applying the preceding estimates gives

\[\begin{aligned}\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|^2&=\|d-hv\|^2\\&=\|d\|^2-2h\langle v,d\rangle+h^2\|v\|^2\\&\le(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\|d\|^2.\end{aligned}\]
steps.note:
1. Line 27.

    rw [show ... by module, ...] includes a locally proved equality directly in a rewrite list. The equality rearranges the two Euler steps into (x - y) - h • (gx - gy). show states this equality as a proof-term target, and by module proves it by vector-space algebra. The comma following that proof continues the same rw list. Because there is no at, the target squared norm is being rewritten.

  2. Line 28.

    norm_sub_sq_real expands the squared norm of a difference. real_inner_smul_right extracts the scalar h from the inner product's right input. norm_smul extracts it from the norm, and Real.norm_eq_abs writes its real norm as |h|. These rules turn Hilbert-space expressions into scalar expressions where the two prepared bounds apply. Their order matters because later rules act on expressions introduced by earlier ones.

  3. Line 29.

    abs_of_nonneg hh replaces |h| by h using the step-size proof. ← real_inner_comm (x - y) (gx - gy) swaps the indicated inner product to the orientation used by hmono. The left arrow requests the reversed direction of that equality. The final bracket closes this single multiline rewrite instruction; the norm expansion is now in the desired scalar form.

  4. Line 30.

    nlinarith combines the expanded target with hmonoScaled and hLipScaled. The cross term is subtracted, so the lower bound on the inner product produces an upper bound after multiplication by the negative sign in the expansion. The squared-gradient term is bounded by the scaled Lipschitz inequality. The resulting polynomial is the coefficient in the theorem's conclusion; the tactic checks the scalar combination and closes the proof.

declarations.statement_note:
(x y gx gy : H) is shorthand for four explicit vector arguments of the same type. (m h : ℝ) supplies two real scalars, (L : ℝ≥0) a nonnegative real constant, and (hh : 0 ≤ h) a proof of a nonnegative step size. The hypotheses hmono and hLip are respectively the stated monotonicity and norm bounds for this particular pair of points and vectors. No assumption says that gx or gy is a gradient.

The target is a squared norm inequality. In h • gx, a real scalar acts on a vector; in 2 * h * m, real numbers multiply each other. The factor (L : ℝ) is a coercion to the real value underlying L. The proof first prepares signed scalar inequalities, then expands the vector difference's squared norm, and finishes by arithmetic.

declarations.name: gradient_step_contract
declarations.title: Taking the square root
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\), \(m\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and \(h\ge0\). Assume

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle,\qquad\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|.\]

Then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\,\|x-y\|.\]

No separate sign assumption on \(1-2hm+h^2L^2\) is needed. If \(x=y\), the Lipschitz condition gives \(g_x=g_y\), so the conclusion is zero on both sides. If \(x\ne y\), the squared estimate implies that the coefficient is nonnegative, and ordinary square-root monotonicity applies.

steps.prose: Apply the preceding squared estimate. With \(A=\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\), \(r=\|x-y\|\), and \(c=1-2hm+h^2L^2\), it says \(A^2\le cr^2\).
steps.note:
1. Line 40.

    have hsq := gradient_step_sq_bound x y gx gy m h L hh hmono hLip applies the theorem immediately above. The first four inputs identify the points and arbitrary vector values. The next three are the monotonicity parameter, step size, and nonnegative Lipschitz constant. The final three are proofs of the sign and comparison hypotheses. Spaces indicate successive function application, so the order must match the declaration. Lean infers the ambient vector type and its instances automatically.

    hsq now names the squared conclusion with the same data as the present theorem. No type is explicitly written after its name; Lean infers it from this application. The current goal still asks for a norm bound involving a square root. Reusing this established squared theorem keeps the vector expansion in one place and makes the remaining argument entirely about ordered real numbers and the real square root.

steps.prose:
Since \(A\ge0\), take square roots and use \(r^2\ge0\):

\[A\le\sqrt{cr^2}=\sqrt c\,\sqrt{r^2}=\sqrt c\,r.\]

The square-root product identity is valid here even without a sign hypothesis on \(c\), because the second factor \(r^2\) is nonnegative.

1. Line 41.

    Real.le_sqrt_of_sq_le hsq turns the squared comparison into an upper bound by the square root of its right side. The resulting fact hbound bounds the Euler-step norm by Real.sqrt (coefficient * ‖x - y‖ ^ 2). The theorem is designed for real square roots; it does not require us to separately assert that the coefficient itself is positive. The whole right side is known to dominate a square by hsq.

  2. Line 42.

    rwa [...] at hbound means “rewrite at hbound, then try to finish by an existing matching assumption.” Real.sqrt_mul' _ (sq_nonneg _) separates the square root of a product using nonnegativity of the squared-distance factor; the underscores are placeholders Lean fills from the surrounding expression, not omitted proof obligations. After these rewrites, hbound is exactly the target inequality, and rwa uses it to close the goal. The suffix a is the assumption-closing part of this tactic.

declarations.statement_note:
(x y gx gy : H) is shorthand for four explicit vector arguments of the same type. (m h : ℝ) supplies two real scalars, (L : ℝ≥0) a nonnegative real constant, and (hh : 0 ≤ h) a proof of a nonnegative step size. The hypotheses hmono and hLip are respectively the stated monotonicity and norm bounds for this particular pair of points and vectors. No assumption says that gx or gy is a gradient.

The target is a norm inequality with the real square root of the preceding coefficient. Real.sqrt is defined for every real input, returning zero for nonpositive inputs. This theorem needs no separate sign assumption on that coefficient; it derives the result from the available squared bound. In h • gx, a real scalar acts on a vector; in 2 * h * m, real numbers multiply each other. The factor (L : ℝ) is a coercion to the real value underlying L. The proof reuses the squared bound, applies a square-root comparison theorem, and simplifies the square root of the squared distance.

sections.setup_note:
This file imports real inner-product identities, real square-root identities, and the arithmetic/vector tactics used below. open scoped NNReal enables notation for the nonnegative real type ℝ≥0. namespace ULA prefixes its declarations by ULA.. The ambient vector type H carries a normed commutative additive group and real inner product through square-bracket instance binders. Completeness is not required here: the arguments gx and gy are arbitrary vectors, and this file does not construct gradients from derivatives.

When reading an application such as gradient_step_sq_bound x y gx gy m h L hh hmono hLip, the first arguments are data and the last arguments are proofs, but all are ordinary inputs to the theorem. Lean checks each input's type in order. L : ℝ≥0 stores nonnegativity, while (L : ℝ) is the real value used in a formula; hh : 0 ≤ h separately supplies the sign of the real step size.

sections.title: The Langevin update and cancellation under shared noise
sections.intro: For \(E_d=\mathbb R^d\), potential \(U\), step \(h\), and innovation \(z\), define \(T_h^z(x)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\). When the same innovation is used at \(x\) and \(y\), subtraction cancels the two noise increments. The distance between updates is therefore bounded by the deterministic Euler estimate. This comparison holds for each noise vector and does not require Gaussianity or independence. If \(h>0\) and the innovation is standard Gaussian, its scaled covariance is \(2hI_d\).

declarations.name: E
declarations.title: The Euclidean state space
declarations.statement: For \(d\in\mathbb N\), let \(E_d=\mathbb R^d\) with the Euclidean inner product. Its coordinates are indexed by \(0,\ldots,d-1\). When \(d=0\), the index set is empty and the space consists of its zero vector.

steps.prose:
Identify a vector with its coordinate tuple. The norm is

\[\|x\|=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_i^2\right)^{1/2}.\]

The gradient and distance estimates below use this inner-product norm.
steps.note:
1. Line 14.

    abbrev E (d : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) declares the reusable name E with one explicit natural-number input. (d : ℕ) is a binder: its name is available on the right of :=, and its type is the natural numbers. := introduces the abbreviation's defining value, here a type. EuclideanSpace takes the scalar type ℝ and coordinate-index type Fin d as arguments. The parentheses around Fin d ensure that this whole applied type is the second argument.

    An abbrev is readily unfolded by Lean when checking types, so the library's Euclidean norm, inner product, and completeness instances remain available for E d. This is different from declaring a vector variable or a proof hypothesis. As a concrete reading example, x : E 2 means a real vector with two Euclidean coordinates, indexed by the two members of Fin 2. The line contains the complete declaration; no separate proof follows it.

declarations.statement_note:
abbrev introduces a transparent abbreviation rather than a proposition needing a proof. E is a type-valued function: it takes a natural number d and returns the type of Euclidean vectors of that dimension. ℕ includes zero. Thus E 3 names three-dimensional Euclidean space, and a binder (x : E d) says that x is one vector in the selected dimension.

EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) is Mathlib's finite-coordinate real inner-product space. Fin d is the type of natural numbers strictly less than d, used to index coordinates. The choice of EuclideanSpace equips those coordinates with the Euclidean norm and inner product. One should not replace it indiscriminately by a bare function type, whose default norm structure may be different. There is no := by because this line defines a type rather than proving a theorem.

declarations.name: ulaUpdate
declarations.title: One unadjusted Langevin step
declarations.statement:
For a potential \(U:E_d\to\mathbb R\), a real step size \(h\), a state \(x\in E_d\), and a noise vector \(z\in E_d\), define

\[T_h^z(x)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z.\]

The definition itself imposes no sign condition on \(h\); later contraction results assume \(h\ge0\).

steps.prose: The update consists of the current state, the drift increment \(-h\nabla U(x)\), and the noise increment \(\sqrt{2h}\,z\).
steps.note:
1. Line 18.

    x - h • gradient U x + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • z is the defining value of ulaUpdate U h x z. The header already supplied def, the argument binders, output type, and :=; this line supplies its body. Lean parses gradient U x as the gradient of the function U at the vector x. Function application binds more tightly than •, so h • gradient U x means scalar multiplication of that whole gradient vector, not application of h • gradient as a function.

    Real.sqrt (2 * h) is a real scalar; the parentheses make the product 2 * h its input. Its scalar action on z is the noise increment. Addition and subtraction combine vectors of type E d. The two symbols * and • have distinct roles: real multiplication versus real action on vectors. This is an expression defining an output, with no tactic or proof goal involved. The library's gradient is used abstractly; defining this update does not compute a concrete derivative formula for U.

declarations.statement_note:
def ulaUpdate defines a function. {d : ℕ} is its inferred dimension argument, followed by explicit arguments (U : E d → ℝ), the potential, (h : ℝ), the step size, and (x z : E d), the current state and noise vector. The final : E d specifies that the output is another vector in the same space. The := at the end of the declaration header introduces the formula displayed in the step below.

There is no differentiability or positivity hypothesis in this definition. Mathlib's gradient and Real.sqrt are total mathematical functions, so the expression has a type for every stated input. Later theorems add analytic hypotheses to establish useful properties. The same noise vector z can be supplied to updates from two different starting states, which is the coupling used in the following cancellation lemma.

declarations.name: ulaUpdate_sub
declarations.title: Shared noise cancels
declarations.statement:
For every potential \(U:E_d\to\mathbb R\), \(h\in\mathbb R\), and vectors \(x,y,z\in E_d\),

\[T_h^z(x)-T_h^z(y)=(x-h\nabla U(x))-(y-h\nabla U(y)).\]

steps.prose:
Expand the two updates. The two copies of \(\sqrt{2h}\,z\) subtract to zero:

\[(x-h abla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z)-(y-h abla U(y)+\sqrt{2h}\,z)=(x-h abla U(x))-(y-h abla U(y)).\]
steps.note:
1. Line 24.

    simp only [ulaUpdate, add_sub_add_right_eq_sub] closes the vector equality. The entry ulaUpdate tells the simplifier to unfold both instances of the defined update. After unfolding, both vectors contain exactly the same final term Real.sqrt (2 * h) • z. The library equality add_sub_add_right_eq_sub cancels a common term added on the right: an expression of the form (a + c) - (b + c) becomes a - b.

    The square brackets are a simplification list, mixing a definition to unfold with a theorem to rewrite by. only restricts the simplifier to this list and basic reductions, making the intended cancellation explicit. There is no at clause, so the tactic acts on the current goal. Once both sides match, it finishes the proof. The fact that this works for an arbitrary z is stronger than a statement about one particular sampled noise value; probability has not entered yet.

declarations.statement_note:
lemma ulaUpdate_sub {d : ℕ} ... states an equality of vectors, with dimension inferred from the explicit potential and vector arguments. (x y z : E d) provides two starting points and one common noise vector. The same z appears in ulaUpdate U h x z and ulaUpdate U h y z; that shared input is the reason cancellation works.

The target equality removes the matching noise increments and leaves a difference of two gradient steps. Parentheses on the right group each whole step, so its subtraction is unambiguous. No assumptions about a Gaussian distribution, differentiability, convexity, or the sign of h are needed for this algebraic identity. := by begins the proof, which unfolds the definition and uses an additive-group cancellation equality.

declarations.name: ula_shared_noise_contract
declarations.title: The initial shared-noise estimate
declarations.statement:
Suppose \(U:E_d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\), and \(h\ge0\). For every \(x,y,z\in E_d\),

\[\|T_h^z(x)-T_h^z(y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\,\|x-y\|.\]

For \(h>0\) this factor is strictly below one whenever \(hL^2<2m\).

steps.prose: Cancel the common noise. The left-hand side becomes the distance between the two deterministic gradient steps.
steps.note:
1. Line 45.

    rw [ulaUpdate_sub] applies the cancellation lemma from the preceding declaration inside the main target's norm. A rewrite can replace a subexpression inside a larger expression, so an equality of vectors may be used directly under norm signs. The two ulaUpdate calls share U,h,z, making the lemma match. Lean infers its dimension and vector arguments from the occurrence in the goal.

    After the rewrite, the left side is the norm of (x - h • gradient U x) - (y - h • gradient U y). The right side is unchanged. This transformation leaves exactly the deterministic gradient-step shape required by the imported theorem. The brackets contain one theorem used as a rewrite rule. No local fact is targeted with at, so the current goal changes. This step uses only algebraic equality and does not inspect the value or distribution of the shared noise vector.

steps.prose:
Strong convexity gives

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle abla U(x)- abla U(y),x-y angle,\]

and the Lipschitz assumption gives \(\| abla U(x)- abla U(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Insert these two inequalities into the Euler-step square-root bound.
steps.note:
1. Line 46.

    exact ULA.gradient_step_contract ... begins an application of the imported deterministic theorem. The namespace prefix ULA. identifies which declaration is meant. x y are its starting points, (gradient U x) and (gradient U y) instantiate its arbitrary vector inputs, and m h L hh supply the parameters and nonnegative-step proof. The parentheses group each gradient value as one argument. The theorem still needs its monotonicity and Lipschitz hypotheses, supplied by the next two lines.

  2. Line 47.

    ULA.strong_gradient_monotone hdiff hsc x y produces exactly the required monotonicity inequality from differentiability and strong convexity of U. The parentheses make the entire theorem application one proof argument of gradient_step_contract. Euclidean completeness and inner-product structures are inferred by typeclass search, rather than passed manually as ordinary positional inputs.

  3. Line 48.

    (by simpa only [dist_eq_norm] using hsm.dist_le_mul x y) supplies the final proof argument. The Lipschitz proof hsm gives a distance inequality at x,y; dist_eq_norm converts both distances to the corresponding norms of differences. simpa only then closes this small local goal. With all hypotheses supplied, the outer exact has the same type as the rewritten target and completes the theorem. The formula thus follows for every shared z from the deterministic estimate.

declarations.statement_note:
The theorem takes a potential U : E d → ℝ, real parameters m,h, and L : ℝ≥0. Its proof inputs are hdiff for differentiability, hsc for strong convexity on the universal set, hsm for LipschitzWith L (gradient U), and hh for 0 ≤ h. The explicit vectors x,y,z are arbitrary, with z shared by both updates. The dimension is implicit.

The conclusion bounds their distance by the earlier square-root coefficient times the starting distance. ‖...‖ is a norm of a vector difference; the factor containing Real.sqrt is real. Imported deterministic lemmas supply both the analytic monotonicity fact and the Euler-step bound. The proof first rewrites the updates using exact noise cancellation, then supplies those lemmas' inputs. It establishes a pointwise estimate for every noise vector, before selecting any probability law.

sections.setup_note:
The first imports make the deterministic Euler estimate and strong-gradient monotonicity available under the namespace ULA. Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.PiL2 supplies the Euclidean inner-product structure, while the Lipschitz import supplies metric formulations of the smoothness assumption. noncomputable section permits the gradient-based update as a mathematical definition without providing an executable gradient algorithm. open scoped NNReal enables the nonnegative-real notation.

This file is not inside namespace ULA. Consequently E, ulaUpdate, and ulaUpdate_sub are global names here, while imported lemmas are called explicitly as ULA.gradient_step_contract and ULA.strong_gradient_monotone. Euclidean space has the real normed inner-product and completeness instances required by those lemmas; Lean finds those structures through typeclass search. {d : ℕ} in later declarations is an inferred natural-number dimension, whereas x,y,z : E d are vectors in that dimension.

sections.title: The sharp deterministic contraction
sections.intro:
Suppose the same differentiable potential has strong-convexity constant \(m\) and gradient Lipschitz constant \(L\), with \(m\le L\). The quadratic lower and upper inequalities imply \(mL\|d\|^2+\|v\|^2\le(m+L)\langle v,d\rangle\), where \(d=x-y\) and \(v=\nabla U(x)-\nabla U(y)\). Completing the square gives \(\|v-(m+L)d/2\|\le(L-m)\|d\|/2\).

Decompose \(d-hv\) using this center. The triangle inequality gives \((|1-h(m+L)/2|+h(L-m)/2)\|d\|\). For \(m+L>0\), its factor is \(1-mh\) when \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\), and \(Lh-1\) when \(h\ge2/(m+L)\). At \(m=L\), the completed-square radius is zero, so no division by \(L-m\) is needed.

declarations.name: cocoercive_of_quadratic_models
declarations.title: Cocoercivity from two quadratic models
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(f:H\to\mathbb R\), \(g:H\to H\), and \(K\ge0\). Suppose that for all \(a,b\in H\),

\[f(a)+\langle g(a),b-a\rangle\le f(b)\le f(a)+\langle g(a),b-a\rangle+\frac K2\|b-a\|^2.\]

Then for all \(x,y\),

\[\|g(x)-g(y)\|^2\le K\langle g(x)-g(y),x-y\rangle.\]

The proof includes \(K=0\), and does not separately assume that \(g\) is a gradient.

steps.prose:
Fix \(a,b\), \(t\ge0\), and set \(v=g(a)-g(b)\), \(z=a-tv\). Compare the lower model based at \(b\) with the upper model based at \(a\), both evaluated at \(z\):

\[f(b)+\langle g(b),z-b\rangle\le f(z)\le f(a)+\langle g(a),z-a\rangle+\frac K2\|z-a\|^2.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 33.

    have hbregman (a b : H) (t : ℝ) (ht : 0 ≤ t) : introduces a reusable local theorem, with two vector arguments, a real step parameter, and a proof of its sign. These binders let the same estimate later be applied to both point orders. The name hbregman is chosen by the author to suggest the objective's supporting-plane gap; it is not a built-in tactic. Its proposition spans the next two lines.

  2. Line 34.

    This is the left side of the intermediate inequality: a scalar coefficient t - K / 2 * t ^ 2, written distributively, multiplying the squared norm of the field difference. g a and g b are vector values because g : H → H. Norm bars and squaring turn their difference into a real quantity, so all * operations on this line are real multiplication.

  3. Line 35.

    The right side f a - f b - inner ℝ (g b) (a - b) is the objective value at a minus its supporting-plane prediction based at b. The final := by opens the nested proof of this whole inequality. The type of the real inner product is inferred from the vectors and explicit scalar field ℝ.

  4. Line 36.

    let z := a - t • (g a - g b) defines the trial vector. Lean infers its type H. The parentheses keep the field difference together under scalar action by t. This local definition is available only inside the proof of hbregman, and it can be unfolded below using dsimp [z]. No existence theorem is required: the formula directly gives the vector we need.

  5. Line 37.

    have hl := hlower b z specializes the universal lower model at base point b and endpoint z. Its inferred proposition is f b + inner ℝ (g b) (z - b) ≤ f z. The short name hl keeps this inequality available for later rewriting and arithmetic; the current goal remains the intermediate gap estimate.

  6. Line 38.

    have hu := hupper a z specializes the upper model at base point a and the same endpoint z. It bounds f z by f a, a linear term, and the quadratic error. Having a lower and upper estimate of the same f z permits that unknown function value to be eliminated by combining the inequalities.

steps.prose: The displacements are \(z-a=-tv\) and \(z-b=(a-b)-tv\). Substitute them into the two models. Since \(t\ge0\), the quadratic term is \(\|z-a\|^2=t^2\|v\|^2\).
steps.note:
1. Line 39.

    have hz₁ : z - a = -t • (g a - g b) := by dsimp [z]; module proves the first displacement formula. hz₁ is an identifier with a Unicode subscript one. dsimp [z] unfolds the trial-point definition; the semicolon sequences the tactic that follows on the generated goals, and module verifies vector-space algebra. The minus on t is scalar negation before scalar action.

  2. Line 40.

    have hz₂ : z - b = (a - b) - t • (g a - g b) := by ... proves the displacement from the other base point. Again, unfolding followed by module checks the identity. hz₂ is a proof of an equality, whereas z itself is a defined vector. Both sorts of local names can later occur inside rewrite or simplifier lists, with different roles.

  3. Line 41.

    rw [hz₂, inner_sub_right, real_inner_smul_right] at hl substitutes the second displacement formula in the lower model. The next rule distributes its inner product over the subtraction, and the final rule pulls the real scalar t outside. at hl directs these changes to the stored lower inequality rather than the goal. The unknown f z remains until arithmetic combines the two models.

  4. Line 42.

    rw [hz₁, real_inner_smul_right, norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, ...] at hu starts normalization of the upper model using the first displacement formula. It extracts -t from the inner product and norm, then converts the scalar norm to absolute value. The single rewrite list continues onto the next source line.

  5. Line 43.

    abs_neg turns |-t| into |t|; abs_of_nonneg ht then turns it into t using the explicit parameter-sign proof. The closing at hu applies the full list to the upper-model fact. This explains exactly where the assumption ht : 0 ≤ t is used. The squared norm term is now a scalar expression involving t ^ 2 and the squared field difference.

steps.prose:
The difference of the linear terms satisfies

\[\langle g(a),v\rangle-\langle g(b),v\rangle=\|v\|^2.\]

Eliminating \(f(z)\) therefore gives

\[\left(t-\frac K2t^2\right)\|g(a)-g(b)\|^2\le f(a)-f(b)-\langle g(b),a-b\rangle.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 44.

    have hi : inner ℝ (g a) (g a - g b) - inner ℝ (g b) (g a - g b) = starts an auxiliary real equality. Both inner products have the same second argument, so their difference can be combined into an inner product of the difference of their first arguments. The right side of the equality follows on the next line.

  2. Line 45.

    ‖g a - g b‖ ^ 2 := by gives that equality's right side and begins its proof. This is precisely the squared field difference appearing in both the desired bound and the model error. Naming this identity allows the subsequent arithmetic tactic to recognize a geometric cancellation it would not derive by itself.

  3. Line 46.

    rw [← inner_sub_left, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] first uses linearity backwards to combine the two inner products into inner ℝ (g a - g b) (g a - g b). The second identity turns a self-inner-product into a squared norm. The left arrow affects the first rule only. These rewrites close the equality hi.

  4. Line 47.

    nlinarith now combines hl, hu, and hi as real polynomial information. The shared quantity f z cancels, while the linear field terms contribute a multiple of the squared difference. The result is the stated hbregman estimate. This finishes the nested proof, making the local theorem usable at arbitrary later choices of a,b,t and sign proof ht.

steps.prose: Apply this estimate to \((a,b)=(x,y)\) and \((y,x)\), with the same \(t\ge0\). Adding will cancel the function values.
steps.note:
1. Line 48.

    have hsum (t : ℝ) (ht : 0 ≤ t) : declares another local theorem, this time for the fixed outer points x,y and every nonnegative step parameter. The vector pair is no longer a binder on hsum: it is inherited from the enclosing theorem. Later hsum 1 ... and hsum K⁻¹ ... specialize only the real parameter and its sign proof.

  2. Line 49.

    The left side adds the two ordered-pair estimates, producing coefficients 2 * t and K * t ^ 2 multiplying the same squared field difference. Every operation on this line is real scalar arithmetic after evaluating the vector norm. Its type is completed by the inequality's right side below.

  3. Line 50.

    The right side is inner ℝ (g x - g y) (x - y), the scalar pairing needed in the final cocoercivity conclusion. := by begins the proof of this estimate. Unlike the earlier supporting-plane gaps, this expression contains no objective values, because those will cancel between the two point orders.

  4. Line 51.

    have hxy := hbregman x y t ht applies the reusable gap estimate with the outer points in their original order. It passes the same real t and proof ht introduced for hsum. The result is a known inequality, named for the x,y order.

  5. Line 52.

    have hyx := hbregman y x t ht applies it again in the reverse order. This second fact has the reversed field difference and displacement; both must be normalized before the two inequalities visibly combine. The objective differences occur with opposite signs, providing the cancellation used next.

steps.prose:
The two gradient norms are equal and the reversed displacement changes the sign of its inner product. Thus, writing \(A=\|g(x)-g(y)\|^2\) and \(B=\langle g(x)-g(y),x-y\rangle\), we have for every \(t\ge0\),

\[(2t-Kt^2)A\le B.\]
steps.note:
1. Line 53.

    rw [norm_sub_rev] at hyx uses symmetry of the norm under reversing a subtraction. Lean infers the arguments from the occurrence in the reverse-order estimate. This makes the squared field-difference norm in hyx match the one in hxy. Rewriting within a squared expression is permitted because equal subexpressions can be substituted anywhere in a formula.

  2. Line 54.

    rw [← neg_sub x y, inner_neg_right] at hyx turns the reversed displacement y - x into the negative of x - y, then moves its negation outside the inner product. Explicit arguments to neg_sub select the point difference rather than the field difference. The left arrow requests the backward orientation of this equality.

  3. Line 55.

    rw [inner_sub_left] expands the target's inner product of g x - g y. Because no at clause is present, it changes the current hsum goal. This makes its gradient terms appear separately, in the same form as those in the two prepared inequalities.

  4. Line 56.

    linarith adds and rearranges the two estimates. The objective values cancel, two copies of the step-linear contribution combine, and two half-quadratic contributions make the full K term. The local theorem hsum is established for every nonnegative t. The next blocks choose particular t values depending on whether K is zero or strictly positive.

steps.prose: First consider \(K=0\). Taking \(t=1\) gives \(2A\le B\). As \(A\ge0\), this also shows \(B\ge0\).
steps.note:
1. Line 57.

    rcases hK.eq_or_lt with hzero | hpos splits 0 ≤ K into its equality and strict-inequality alternatives. Dot notation invokes the order theorem on the existing proof hK. rcases ... with ... | ... destructs the resulting disjunction, naming the zero-case equality hzero in one branch and the proof 0 < K as hpos in the other. The branches have separate local contexts.

  2. Line 58.

    The bullet · selects the equality case. subst K uses the available equality to replace the parameter K by zero throughout that branch's goal and context. This substitution makes the requested bound a claim that the squared field difference is at most zero. We do not divide by K in this branch.

  3. Line 59.

    have h := hsum 1 (by norm_num) specializes the parameter estimate at t = 1. The inline by norm_num proves that one is nonnegative. Since K has been replaced by zero, the useful content is 2 * ‖g x - g y‖ ^ 2 ≤ inner ℝ (g x - g y) (x - y). Lean infers the full type of h.

  4. Line 60.

    have hmono : 0 ≤ inner ℝ (g x - g y) (x - y) := by requests nonnegativity of the inner-product quantity. This sign fact will ensure that the specially chosen numerator inner ... + 1 is positive in the contradiction argument. It is being deduced from the parameter estimate, not assumed separately.

  5. Line 61.

    nlinarith [sq_nonneg ‖g x - g y‖] combines h with nonnegativity of the squared norm. The expression after sq_nonneg is itself a real norm, so its square is nonnegative by general real arithmetic. It follows that the upper quantity in h is nonnegative, proving hmono. This closes just the nested sign proof; the zero-curvature branch still needs to show that the squared norm vanishes.

steps.prose:
If the desired conclusion \(A\le0\) were false, then \(A>0\). We could choose

\[t=\frac{B+1}{2A}\ge0.\]

The estimate \(2tA\le B\) would then force \(B+1\le B\).
steps.note:
1. Line 62.

    by_contra hn switches the zero-curvature branch to proof by contradiction. It introduces hn, the negation of the desired squared-norm inequality, and changes the current target to False. All previously proved estimates remain available. We will show the alleged strictly positive squared norm contradicts the estimate that holds for every nonnegative t.

  2. Line 63.

To justify that substitution, \(A>0\) implies \(\|g(x)-g(y)\|\ne0\), so its square can be cancelled from the denominator. Hence indeed

\[2\frac{B+1}{2A}A=B+1.\]

    have heq : 2 * ((inner ... + 1) / starts the cancellation equality for the selected quotient. Its expression continues across the following lines; the newline does not terminate a declaration with an unfinished type. heq will justify exactly the substitution needed in hh. Division identities require a nonzero denominator, which will be proved inside this local block.

The resulting left side is the twice-parameter-times-squared-norm expression whose value was proved in heq.

Now suppose \(K>0\). Choose \(t=K^{-1}\) in the common estimate:

\[\frac AK\le B.\]

declarations.statement_note:
The explicit functions are f : H → ℝ, a real-valued objective, and g : H → H, an arbitrary vector field. K : ℝ is a real curvature parameter, and hK : 0 ≤ K is a separate proof of its sign.
